title: Blockset throttle: KV telemetry and GPU-swap simulator for paged KV
creator: Ava Chen
description: Implement a blockset-oriented throttling layer and an offline+online GPU-swap simulator to validate heuristics for paged/blocked KV cache behavior under continuous batching workloads. Deliverables: (1) a lightweight in-prod telemetry schema (blockset-level residency, eviction latencies, swap IO distribution), (2) an offline simulator that models PCIe/NVMe swap cost and batching-aware eviction, and (3) a small runtime patch that applies 'blockset-throttle' signals to reduce OOM spikes and smoothing eviction pressure during bursty token streams.
background: We observe short high-throughput bursts from continuous batching that cause focused hotset churn and sudden GPU-residency pressure. Existing page-by-page eviction yields high IO amplification and long tail latencies when multiple batches touch overlapping token-affinity ranges. Prior tickets explored slab allocation, prefetch hints, and chunking; here we aim to combine a blockset grouping + telemetry-driven throttle so runtime can smooth swap traffic and make smarter demotion decisions.
design_decision_log:
Decisions so far:
- Grouping: KV entries will be grouped into blocksets sized to 256KB–1MB depending on model shard density. This gives a trade-off between IO granularity and eviction precision.
- Throttle signal: compute a moving window pressure metric (blockset_pressure) that combines resident_fraction, recent_eviction_rate, and recent_swap_ms. Use a PID-inspired controller to derive a throttle factor between 0.0–1.0 applied to background eviction and prefetch budgets.
- Hotset smoothing: when continuous-batching rate exceeds configured rps_threshold, temporarily increase prefetch aggressiveness for blocksets with token-affinity > 0.6 while throttling global background compaction to avoid IO spikes.
- Simulator model: offline simulator to accept traces (request KV keys + timestamps + batch_id) and simulate different blockset sizes, swap device latencies (PCIe 8GB/s, NVMe 3GB/s), and concurrency limits.
Rationale: grouping reduces number of IO ops and improves spatial locality; throttle reduces sawtooth swap behavior during bursty traffic; simulator provides safe tuning before rolling to customers.
implementation_plan:
Phase 1 (telemetry + traces, 1 sprint): add blockset-level counters (resident_bytes, evicted_bytes, avg_swap_ms, last_touch_ts) to the runtime telemetry exporter. Add a lightweight trace capture mode for 1% of requests to record KV key touch sequences.
Phase 2 (simulator + analysis, 2–3 weeks): build a Rust-based offline simulator that can replay traces and evaluate metrics (swap-threshold crossings, P95 latency uplift, IO amplification). Provide a small DSL to vary blockset size and device parameters.
Phase 3 (runtime throttle, 1 sprint): implement the throttle controller inside the KV manager. The controller computes per-tenant throttle and per-blockset budget. Integrate with continuous-batching scheduler to reduce prefetch when throttle>0.6.
Phase 4 (canary + telemetry validation, 2 cycles): run canary on internal tenants with heavy batching profiles, monitor swap latencies and tail-latency regression, iterate.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Telemetry exported and visible in internal console panels for blockset metrics.
2) Simulator can ingest real traces and show measurable IO amplification differences between blockset sizes.
3) Runtime throttle reduces 99th-percentile swap IO ops by at least 30% in internal canary runs without increasing request P99 generation latency by more than 5%.
4) No functional regressions in continuous-batching correctness; KV hits/misses convergent to baseline after stabilization window.
test_plan:
- Unit tests: blockset mapping, controller math, and budget enforcement.
- Simulator tests: deterministic trace replays with mocked device latencies to validate expected IO counts.
- Integration: deploy to a dedicated canary stack running long-tail batching workloads (internal benchmark harness). Record baseline then enable throttle. Compare metrics: swap ops/s, NVMe bandwidth, GPU memory OOMs, generation tail latencies.
- Chaos tests: synthetic traffic spikes that exceed batch-rate thresholds and verify throttle prevents cascading host swap storms.
rollout_plan:
- Stage 0: telemetry only (2 days) on canary tenants.
- Stage 1: simulator release to infra team for tuning (1 week).
- Stage 2: runtime throttle behind feature flag; enable for 10% internal traffic (1 week).
- Stage 3: increase to 50% then 100% after no regressions.
Rollback: policy to disable throttle flag immediately and run compensating aggressive prefetch temporarily to restore hit rates if latency regressions >5%.
metrics: Primary metrics to monitor: blockset_swap_ops_per_minute, blockset_avg_swap_ms, nvme_bandwidth_utilization, gpu_oom_events, generation_p99_latency_by_tenant. Secondary: prefetch_hit_rate, eviction_io_amplification_ratio.
risks:
- Overly large blockset sizes could increase unnecessary swap of cold entries and hurt cache efficiency.
- PID-like controller may oscillate if window sizes not tuned to workload timescales.
- Telemetry sampling at 1% may miss rare pathological patterns; need adjustable sampling.
- Simulator fidelity: inaccurate device models yield bad knobs in production.
